newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish jobless data down again in election runup.
newsitem.headline: Irish jobless data down again in election runup.

text.p: Irish unemployment, the black spot of an otherwise buoyant economy, fell again in December, giving Prime Minister John Bruton's coalition government a boost in an election year.
Official data showed that the number of people claiming unemployment benefit in December fell to an adjusted 267,000 from 268,700 in November and 282,300 one year ago.

It was the fifth consecutive month in which the dole queue had shortened and supported government claims that 1996 was a record year for job creation. Bruton's left-right coalition must contest a general election before November and is certain to use its job creation policies as a major plank in its campaign to be returned to office.
The government says that sound financial policies have created unmatched economic growth in the European Union averaging six per cent and tax cuts are widely expected in a budget on January 22.

The coalition, in power since November 1995 when the previous government collapsed, says job creation has been its highest priority and it has aggressively sold Ireland as a location for foreign investment, especially in the hi-tech and computer sector.
The government has also cracked down on social security fraud which a government survey suggested was widespread with people claiming unemployment benefit and holding jobs in many areas.
Unemployment rose slightly in two months in 1996 but the overall trend has been down and Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn estimates that 50,000 jobs were created last year.

The last published percentage breakdown of Irish unemployment was for April and put the rate at 11.9 percent, one of the highest in the European Union where Spain, Finland and France top the dole data.
But Irish unemployment is expected to dip below 11 percent in 1997 for the first time in years, the independent Economic and Social Research Institute said in its latest report.
"Since April 1991, the total number at work has increased by 150,000 or 13.2 percent, with 136,000 of that increase taking place since April 1993 and 45,000 in the year to April 1996," it said.
Bruton's Fine Gael party and its junior Labour and Democratic Left allies are expected to call an election soon after the budget with May tipped as the most likely month.
